# Design decisions

32 records: 32 active, 0 superseded.

Each record is what this project chose and why, on the information available at the time.
It is not evidence. `README.md` says how a record is written and revised. Every record names
in `revisit if` what would make it worth reopening.

## Active

- **[address-spaces-as-objects](./address-spaces-as-objects/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-06): A space is a retyped object of kind process, IO or nested; its table pages come from an untyped named in the map call; a frame entry's mapping node sits at a fixed index in the table page's block so it is found in constant time; a child table's hidden node is its entry's node; PCIDs and ASIDs recycle per core by generation, an IOid is fixed per device.
  - *confidence:* Structural; the table-page layout and the entry-record agreement are proven in kernel/verified/capability/space.rs, link.rs and mapping.rs.
  - *revisit if:* A space kind appears whose entries cannot carry a node at a fixed index, or a device must change IOid while bound.
- **[arch-module](./arch-module/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): The page size, the entries a level, the level count and the block sizes are the target's, any power of two its translation format offers; both targets run 4K pages, 512 entries a level and four levels today, written as literals the proofs still assume. An entry's bit layout is per-ISA, including where the walker sets accessed and dirty and whether it does. A per-ISA arch module, selected by cfg(target_arch) with no traits, supplies six items: page-entry encoding, trap frame and user-return checks, address-space switch and flush token, syscall register table, exception and interrupt entry glue, and the IOMMU command ring with its invalidate token. Platform glue is a separate per-machine crate.
  - *confidence:* What each granule fixes is arithmetic on the Arm ARM's VMSAv8-64 translation formats; that the proofs can take the granule as a parameter is untested, since today they are written over 4K literals. That six items suffice held for the second target: aarch64 under QEMU virt verifies against the same specs and boots dom0 in atmo test with no item beyond them.
  - *revisit if:* A translation regime the project must use takes a page that is not a power of two, a workload needs more than 48 bits of VA (x86 LA57, Arm LPA2), or a second implementation of an item has to coexist on one target, such as a second kind of IOMMU (VT-d beside AMD-Vi, DART beside SMMUv3), which is when a trait starts to pay.
- **[capability-names-a-block](./capability-names-a-block/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): A memory capability names a block: a base aligned to its size and 2^order pages. Frames retype at 4K or 2M in constant time, a 2M frame derives 4K pieces, and a map names a capability, a page offset and an address, so a pager needs few slots.
  - *confidence:* Arithmetic on the page table's block sizes; the payload well-formedness is proven in kernel/verified/capability/table.rs.
  - *revisit if:* A workload needs frames that are not power-of-two aligned, or the 1G frame that pagetable does not yet map becomes necessary rather than convenient.
- **[cpu-time-as-capability](./cpu-time-as-capability/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-05): Per-core run queues, fixed priorities, turns at equal priority, one selection function and one scheduling record per thread. A core capability allows placing a thread on that core at or below its maximum priority, a derived copy may lower it, and a placement is a binding so CPU time is revocable. Budgets and periods are deferred, with three constraints kept so they stay addable.
  - *confidence:* The human's choice to defer scheduling contexts; the estimate that they cost about 600 to 900 lines of code and 2,500 to 4,000 of proof plus a one-time rework of the scheduler and IPC proofs is reasoned from structure, not measured.
  - *revisit if:* A workload needs a bound on how much time a thread can take, which fixed priorities cannot give, or temporal isolation inside a core is wanted by design/isolation-claim/.
- **[cut-over-on-a-branch](./cut-over-on-a-branch/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-05): New proven modules land on main beside the old kernel while boot keeps using the old one. The cut-over is a branch off main: a build feature selects old or new kernel entry and dom0, the branch gate boots both so each syscall is booted in the commit that wires it, the last commits delete the old kernel and the feature, and the branch merges with a merge commit. Main never contains the selection.
  - *confidence:* A process choice by the human after an independent review judged a single landing too large to finish in one round and its parts unable to pass the gate on their own.
  - *revisit if:* The cut-over branch has merged, when this record has done its work and the shim rule in CLAUDE.md applies to the whole tree again.
- **[device-binding-under-the-space-capability](./device-binding-under-the-space-capability/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): Each device has one binding node, a slot of the list's first node page past the list's first node, live exactly while the device is bound. Bind names a device capability and a device space capability in the caller's table and derives the node under the space capability, holding one of the space block's references, so revoking that capability's lineage unbinds the device and delete of it is refused while bound. The binder is the device's only holder, since a device capability does not derive, and every holder of a device space capability reaches what the space maps, so bind grows no reach; moving a bound device grants what its space maps, and mapping into a device space is a grant by the mapper.
  - *confidence:* The node's place, the invariant tying it to the device's record and the space's bound set, and revoke's unbind are proven in kernel/verified/capability/device.rs and revoke.rs; bind is not yet in the tree. That bind grows no reach is arithmetic on the model once a device space's holders reach what it maps; choosing that reading over a narrower one is judgement, argued below.
  - *revisit if:* A device must be bound to two spaces at once (PASID-tagged DMA, where one device walks several tables), which one binding node per device cannot express; or a device capability must derive, which ends the sole-holder argument and makes bind a growth the theorem does not admit.
- **[divider-proven-by-invariant](./divider-proven-by-invariant/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): The rules that divide the machine between tenants are a table of grants with declared overlap, checked by a decidable layout_ok. A Verus-verified user crate establishes an invariant over the kernel's state and that table, with a state per block; with the kernel theorem it bounds each tenant from above by its rows over reach and from below by a capability for each row, and a witness shows it finishes for every layout that fits. Stage one divides at boot and ends dead while still holding; stage two serves create and destroy, then grow and shrink, then forced reclaim and core moves, each handler keeping the invariant.
  - *confidence:* The human's choice among static only, static then dynamic, and dynamic from the start, after a survey of published initialiser and policy proofs (capDL, Boyton's verified initialisation, seL4's integrity and information-flow proofs, take-grant, EROS confinement) and of hypervisors' allocation. The sizes the choice weighed are reasoned from structure, not measured; that the static case can be carried to running code is the published result, and the dynamic case is new ground.
  - *revisit if:* The caller's-view contracts cannot be proven from the kernel's operation specifications at a cost the project will pay, or a handler stage two needs cannot be written to keep one invariant, which is when the dynamic stage is reconsidered and the statement stays the static one.
- **[fan-in-over-private-rings](./fan-in-over-private-rings/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-09): Several untrusted producers feeding one consumer get one aring each, and afanin's scan finds the first ring with a slot available from a start the caller rotates. No word is written by two producers, so a wild index is rejected by its own ring alone and a producer that stops stalls only its own ring. A queue with one shared enqueue cursor is for producers inside one trust domain and is not built until a caller needs its total order.
  - *confidence:* The isolation is proven in afanin/src/lib.rs over aring's proven observe. That the shared cursor cannot reject a peer's store is an argument from the published algorithms' structure, not a proof; the cost comparison is not measured.
  - *revisit if:* A caller inside one trust domain needs one total order across producers, which the scan does not give; or the number of producers grows until a scan over every ring costs more than the shared cursor's contended line, which a measurement would show.
- **[flush-without-waiting](./flush-without-waiting/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): A ghost per-core TLB model holds possibly stale translations keyed by space and core; unmap bumps a flush epoch, sends IPIs to exactly the cores that loaded the space and returns again; each core's handler flushes every context and records its acknowledgement on its own kernel entry; an IOMMU's invalidate waits for its completion inside the glue, since an IOMMU is not a core; retype requires every core's and present IOMMU's acknowledgement to have reached the epoch, a token only flush glue can produce.
  - *confidence:* The no-wait rule is forced by the lock, see reasoning; the epoch comparison and model are in kernel/verified/capability/kernel.rs and kernel/src/flush.rs, with the flush itself counted glue.
  - *revisit if:* The hardware gains a broadcast invalidation the kernel can rely on (this host reports no INVLPGB), a flush that returns again is measured as the cost that dominates unmap, or an IOMMU's completion wait is measured as the longest step under the lock.
- **[ipc-with-reply-object](./ipc-with-reply-object/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-06): Endpoints rendezvous with queues over the intrusive list, so there is no fixed thread bound; a reply is a retyped object named at receive and used once; a blocked receiver's reply and destination slot are stored as indices and resolved through the root pointer at the match; a match skips dead waiters a fixed number per entry.
  - *confidence:* Rendezvous and the explicit reply follow from the CPU-time decision's constraints; resolving at the match is the answer to a memory-safety finding and is a stated invariant.
  - *revisit if:* Scheduling contexts are added, which is what the explicit reply object keeps possible; or a workload needs asynchronous messages with payload, which notifications do not carry.
- **[isolation-claim](./isolation-claim/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-05): The kernel proves spatial isolation: a process affects only what its capabilities reach and gains authority only by grant or retype. It does not claim noninterference or freedom from timing channels, and the claim says so.
  - *confidence:* A scoping choice by the human. Noninterference is the claim the Atmosphere paper proved with unwinding conditions, so it is known to be reachable; timing needs hardware modelling the project does not have.
  - *revisit if:* A workload needs distrusting programs that cannot observe each other through status codes or timing, which is when noninterference or multiple kernel instances become required rather than later.
- **[land-without-regating](./land-without-regating/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): No lock is held across the gate: a change is gated on the main it rebased onto, then rebased again and landed by a fast-forward git refuses when main moved; a clean rebase lands without a second gate, so main's tip may be a composition no gate has run on until the next change is gated on it, and tools/land.py tells that case from a failing change.
  - *confidence:* A bet by the human on a measured cost and an inferred frequency: the lock's waits are measured over one day, the rate of failing compositions is inferred from gate durations over the same day and was zero in 19.
  - *revisit if:* The project enters a release phase, where main's tip must be a gated tree; or compositions that fail become frequent enough that gating bases and finding the pair costs more than the lock's waits did, counted as `fail` lines in logs/gate-ledger against landings.
- **[latest-value-by-three-slot-exchange](./latest-value-by-three-slot-exchange/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-09): amailbox gives one producer and one consumer the latest value through three slots and one atomic word holding the shared slot's index and a fresh bit: publish is one swap, observe is one load and at most one swap, nobody copies the payload or retries, and intermediate values are dropped. It is for two ends that both follow it; across a distrust boundary the path is aring.
  - *confidence:* The permutation, the fresh bit's meaning and the atomic counts are proven in amailbox/src/lib.rs. That three slots are cheaper to prove than Simpson's four is a judgement from the size of each protocol, not a measurement.
  - *revisit if:* Two ends that do not trust each other need the latest value, which a swapped word cannot protect; a caller measures the word sharing a cache line with the slots as its cost; or a target lacks an atomic swap of 32 bits.
- **[machine-glue-below-the-kernel](./machine-glue-below-the-kernel/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): Boot discovery, the console, the interrupt controller and timer, secondary-core start, shutdown and the IOMMU driver live in one crate per machine (machine/pc for the x86_64 PC, machine/virt for aarch64 on QEMU virt), each exporting the same free functions and constants, and machine/virt one more that names the interrupt an IRQ carries, which the x86_64 IDT gives by the vector taken; the kernel depends on the crate its target selects and re-exports it as crate::machine; the crate depends on nothing in kernel/ or kernel/verified, takes cpu indices as arguments, owns the interrupt vectors and its own per-core state, and issues its own MSR and port instructions.
  - *confidence:* A judgement from a survey of kernel/src at 569f164: the item list and signatures follow today's callers. machine/virt tests that the same list fits QEMU virt: its PL011, PSCI power-off, PSCI core start, GICv3 and generic timer items are written to these signatures and run under KVM with two cores, and the list needed one item more, the acknowledgement. The Cargo constraint that rules out one renamed dependency per target was checked with cargo.
  - *revisit if:* Two machines must be supported on one architecture (bare Apple silicon beside QEMU virt), when target_arch no longer selects the crate and a cargo feature or a second build target must; or a machine needs a kernel service at interrupt or boot time that cannot be passed as an argument, which would make the dependency two-way.
- **[multicore-kernel-shape](./multicore-kernel-shape/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-05): A node is a set of cores with one kernel instance and one queue lock; a system may have any number of nodes, laid out at boot; nothing in kernel state is shared between nodes, memory crosses only as a quiescent untyped handoff, and stealing is pager policy.
  - *confidence:* The shape is a judgement against published multicore kernels; the lock numbers below are measured on the host with user-space threads, not this kernel, and its own lock has not been measured.
  - *revisit if:* Lock hold times measured on this kernel make a one-node system's contention a real workload's problem and a smaller node is not the answer, or a workload needs kernel state shared between nodes that a handoff cannot express.
- **[network-stack-proven-at-tier-1](./network-stack-proven-at-tier-1/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): The network protocol stack is tier 1 required, written in Rust inside Verus with no unverified protocol library: wire formats only through combinators proven once, nesting depths fixed in each format, per-packet work bounded linearly in the packet's length by a ghost step counter, each protocol a transition equal to a specification of its RFC state machine, and no allocation per packet.
  - *confidence:* The tier is the human's choice, made 2026-11-10. The five rules are a judgement on how to make a tier-1 stack affordable; the first formats written in the combinators settle whether the per-format proof is as small as expected.
  - *revisit if:* A wire format the stack must accept cannot be written in the combinators under a fixed nesting bound, or a format written in them still needs a proof as large as a hand-written parser's, which reopens rule 1; lowering the tier is the human's decision.
- **[no-gate-for-what-no-step-reads](./no-gate-for-what-no-step-reads/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): tools/land.py lists the paths no gate step reads (.claude/agents/, .claude/skills/, CLAUDE.md); a change that touches nothing else, with no file over the size limit, is rebased, merged and pushed without running the gate, and its tree takes the base's verdict in the ledger.
  - *confidence:* An argument, not a measurement: the gate's result is a function of the files its steps read. That no step reads the listed paths was checked by search on the day, and nothing in the gate keeps it true.
  - *revisit if:* A gate step starts reading a listed path, which removes the path from the list in the same commit; or a main that fails by itself is traced to a commit that landed this way.
- **[one-kernel-instance](./one-kernel-instance/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-05): One kernel instance holds every core of the machine and a process lives inside it; the kernel provides no spanning. Four rules keep a later move to several instances cheap, and breaking one is the human's decision.
  - *confidence:* A staging judgement on top of the multicore shape. That one instance pays almost nothing for the node concept is reasoned from the code, not measured: finding the instance is one per-CPU load and no syscall path gains a check.
  - *revisit if:* Lock contention measured on this kernel is one a real workload would hit, a workload needs distrusting programs separated from the shared lock's timing, or a change would break one of the four rules.
- **[one-lock-bounded-steps](./one-lock-bounded-steps/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-06): All of the Kernel value is under one lock with IF clear from entry to exit; every operation does a bounded amount of work and long work returns again with progress in an object, so the invariant holds at every step boundary and other cores interleave only there; per-CPU state outside the lock is only stacks, GDT and TSS, and only core c writes its own current thread.
  - *confidence:* The non-preemptible rule is in the tree since the interrupt change that made it true; the per-CPU split is stated in kernel/verified/capability/kernel.rs; the step counter bounds the capability list's walks, the flush's IPI loop, the acknowledgement check, the stale-epoch record, the IOMMU invalidate, probe, print, a zeroing step, a small block's typing and freeing, revoke, destroy, the device table, and each arm of a reclaim, not yet a whole entry; the budget's value is unmeasured.
  - *revisit if:* The bounded-step budget measured on this kernel gives a lock hold time a workload cannot tolerate, which is the case for a smaller node rather than for preemption.
- **[process-holds-capabilities](./process-holds-capabilities/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): Capabilities belong to a process, not a thread; its table is a root of 512 pointers in the process object and leaves of 127 slots retyped on demand; no capability names a table and no table holds a table, so the capability graph has no cycles and lookup is constant time. A process is an order-3 block of its table's root, its record and its address space; a thread holds no slots: it is an order-1 block of a node page for its bindings and a page for its record and XSAVE area.
  - *confidence:* A structural choice; the no-cycles property it buys is what rules out the delete-cascade problem Nevill's thesis describes, and the table invariant is proven in kernel/verified/capability/table.rs.
  - *revisit if:* Threads in one process need distinct authority, or a process needs more slots than the two levels give, or a table must be passed as a capability, or a supported core's XSAVE area outgrows the 3072 bytes a thread's record page leaves it.
- **[revoke-by-depth-first-list](./revoke-by-depth-first-list/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-06): All capabilities, mappings and bindings derived from the boot root are one doubly linked list in depth-first order, a child straight after its parent; a node's descendants are the run after it with greater depth, and revoke unlinks leaves of that run a bounded number per kernel entry.
  - *confidence:* Proven in the tree, kernel/verified/capability/list.rs and revoke.rs: derive and unlink in constant time, depth-first order kept, a node is in a run exactly when the run's head is its ancestor, a revoke step removes one such node and nothing outside the run, with a falling measure.
  - *revisit if:* A node needs more than one parent, or a lineage must be reparented, neither of which the list can express; or the 255-link walk to a leaf is measured as the bound that sets the lock hold time.
- **[root-process-at-boot](./root-process-at-boot/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): Boot writes page metadata and creates the root process, thread and table. The root holds at fixed slots untyped capabilities covering free memory as aligned blocks, frame capabilities for dom0's image and stack with the rights they were loaded with, its own process and thread, a capability per core at top priority, interrupts, devices, ports, a console, a power capability, SVM and timers; the list's root is a synthetic node boot sets aside, and the root's boot objects are never retyped.
  - *confidence:* Follows from the kernel allocating nothing after boot: something must hold everything at the start, and only one thing does.
  - *revisit if:* Several kernel instances each need a root, in which case what boot hands each root is the open question recorded with that work; or a second boot-created process is wanted.
- **[schedulers-over-core-partitions](./schedulers-over-core-partitions/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-09): Schedulers are swappable user programs over whole-core partitions handed out as derived core capabilities. A real-time library is the only placer on the cores it holds and runs a cooperative class above a preemptive one; a general scheduler holds the rest, places every runnable thread it owns and lets the kernel preempt. The kernel's fixed-priority selection is unchanged.
  - *confidence:* A judgement by the human between three ways of hosting two policies, informed by published partitioned and core-granting systems. Nothing here is measured on this kernel; the latency bound of an isolated core is the lock's, and its step is not yet measured.
  - *revisit if:* Budgets and periods land, which contain a runaway thread on a shared core; or the kernel gains a block-and-wake event on a placement and per-thread consumed time, which make a scheduler that places one thread per core and owns the quantum (fair share) possible.
- **[sharing-by-derive](./sharing-by-derive/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): The only way to share a capability is derive, a child one depth deeper with rights and range within its parent's; nodes never change ancestor; a move relocates a node without changing its place, within the caller's table, out of a controlled process's table, which is a claim, or into one, which is a placement; delete is refused while a node has children, mappings or bindings.
  - *confidence:* The human's choice among three lifetime packages, with a precedent survey of seL4, NOVA, L4Re, Genode, EROS, Zircon and Barrelfish from their documents. The structure it rests on is proven, design/revoke-by-depth-first-list/.
  - *revisit if:* A service must survive the death of the holder that granted to its clients without a longer-lived parent doing the granting, and claim by a supervisor is not enough.
- **[syscall-abi-in-registers](./syscall-abi-in-registers/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): One entry, by position: the operation number, the capability's slot and five arguments in; a status word (status in its low 16 bits, ok 0, refused 1, unknown 2, again 3, and a badge in the upper 48) and five result words out, each output in the register of the input at its position. A table per target names the registers: syscall on x86_64, svc on aarch64. A send carries five words, four with a grant; the kernel copies nothing from user memory, and larger data goes through shared frames. A place in a space is a virtual address and a level, which the kernel splits into the path. A table position is one word: the index in bits 0 to 15, and in bits 16 to 31 one more than the slot of a process capability with control in the caller's table, or 0 for the caller's own; any higher bit is refused. Inspect, operation 15, returns a held capability's kind, base, order and rights in results 1 to 4. Unmap returns the cleared entry's accessed and dirty bits in results 1 and 2. Probe, operation 17, reads and clears the accessed and dirty bits of up to 64 level 1 entries and returns them as two masks in results 1 and 2. Power-off, operation 18, ends the run through a power capability, with argument 1 saying whether the run succeeded.
  - *confidence:* A packing judgement; each target's preserved set is the one its C convention keeps across a call, the memory operations' positions are counted against the verified functions' parameters in kernel/verified/capability, and the aarch64 table is written from the Arm Architecture Reference Manual; dom0's checks run through it at EL0 under KVM on a Cortex-A76, which tests the positions and that an immediate other than 0 returns unknown.
  - *revisit if:* A message that does not fit five words is on a hot path and the shared-frame ring is measured as its cost, an operation needs more than five argument words, a second entry is needed for a different privilege transition, or a target's instruction leaves fewer than seven registers free to carry an invocation.
- **[teardown-driven-by-retype](./teardown-driven-by-retype/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-08): An object is dead when its references reach zero or, for a process or thread, when destroyed through a control capability; every operation then refuses it. There is no kernel list of dead objects: a retype of the block by the holder of its untyped detaches, then dismantles, a bounded slice per entry, until the block is free. The kernel never kills on its own.
  - *confidence:* The human's choice of who pays, and of the kernel deciding no kill policy, after a precedent survey. The block state machine, references, zeroing, reclaim and two-way detach are in the tree; the dismantle arms land with each object kind.
  - *revisit if:* Memory held by dead objects nobody retypes becomes a real shortage that pager policy cannot collect, or a workload needs the kernel to kill a whole process on a fault.
- **[test-guest-memory](./test-guest-memory/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): The gate, the boot-stack check and the pinned measurement boot a 2.5 GiB guest, and the kernel tracks the pages of addresses 0 to 4 GiB, which hold all of it on the PC, where RAM starts at 0, and on QEMU virt, where it starts at 1 GiB. The firmware allocates from the top of RAM and the loader from the bottom, so boot hands the root one whole 1G untyped, 1 to 2 GiB on the PC and 2 to 3 GiB on virt, which the boot check names per target. The loader's pools, the stacks and dom0's window are sized to what they hold, not to the guest, and the memory map crosses as typed ranges.
  - *confidence:* The pool sizes are judgement from the reservation arithmetic below. That 1 to 2 GiB is wholly free on the PC is a measurement of this firmware's map under this loader, not a guarantee of either; the gate's boots recheck it each time. That 2 to 3 GiB is free on virt is a measurement of the firmware's map alone: no kernel has booted there, and the first boot there settles it.
  - *revisit if:* A functional or performance test needs more RAM than 2.5 GiB; a machine the kernel must run on has RAM at or above 4 GiB, which the kernel does not track; or a firmware or loader change puts an allocation into a machine's free 1G region, which a boot there reports as the 1G untyped missing.
- **[theorem-over-reach](./theorem-over-reach/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): A process can read or write an object only if a capability to it is reachable from its own capabilities; every operation changes objects only by a relation of its kind over that reach; reach grows only by grant or retype. Isolation of disjoint subsystems is a corollary.
  - *confidence:* The statement is the human's choice; the definition and the per-operation shape are in the tree, kernel/verified/capability/reach.rs, and each operation's leaf discharges it as it lands. The composed theorem is not yet proven.
  - *revisit if:* A kernel operation is wanted whose effect cannot be written as a relation over the caller's reach, or a shared object must be reachable without any capability naming it.
- **[thread-bound-at-retype](./thread-bound-at-retype/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): Retyping a thread names a process capability too: the thread capability goes under the untyped and the process binding under the process capability in one step, so the only holder of the new control capability already controls the process and no reach grows. There is no bind operation. Revoking the binding leaves an inert thread that cannot be bound again; its registers stay readable, and its untyped's holder retypes its block.
  - *confidence:* Reasoned over kernel/verified/capability/reach.rs and the landed retype and bind, not yet proven: the widened retype lemma and the fact it needs are named below. That the step grows no reach is arithmetic on the model. Choosing construction over a sole-holder bind, which keeps the same theorem, is judgement.
  - *revisit if:* A workload needs a thread moved to another process without being recreated, carrying its registers in the kernel rather than through its supervisor reading and writing them; or a binding that reach reads must be set on an object that exists before the authority it binds, as a device does, for which the sole-holder rule below is the shape to use instead.
- **[trust-boundary](./trust-boundary/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-10): The kernel's theorem holds whatever a pager does, so a swapped per-application pager needs no assurance for anyone else's safety. Isolation between two subsystems also depends on the component that divided the machine between them; that component is tier 1 by design/divider-proven-by-invariant/, and until its stage-one statement verifies the security claim states the dependence on unproven code.
  - *confidence:* The divider's tier is the human's choice. That the kernel theorem needs nothing of user code is the form of design/theorem-over-reach/.
  - *revisit if:* The divider's stage-one statement verifies, when the claim's dependence becomes the proven statement and this record says so; or the divider's tier is lowered, which is the human's decision.
- **[untyped-memory](./untyped-memory/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-05): Physical memory is held as untyped capabilities and retyped into kernel objects and frames from user space; containers and kernel quotas are gone; mapping, paging and allocation policy live in a standard pager and allocator library an application can swap.
  - *confidence:* A purity judgement by the human with its costs priced and accepted: a user-level memory manager to build, and most of the container-based proof to rewrite.
  - *revisit if:* It follows from the purity principle in CLAUDE.md; it is wrong only if an application class cannot be served by any user-space pager, which would be a reason to revisit the principle, not this record alone.
- **[vmm-over-svm](./vmm-over-svm/DECISION.md)** (2026-11-09): A guest touches only what its nested table maps and what its intercept maps let through. The VMM is an ordinary process; VMRUN needs CPL 0, so the kernel runs it on the VMM's thread, owns the VMCB, and rewrites every control field from the validated request on each run. A nested table is an address space kind for revocation.
  - *confidence:* A design note against AMD APM volume 2 chapter 15 and the host's reported SVM features; no code yet. The run path's register facts (what VMRUN does and does not save) are from the manual.
  - *revisit if:* The VMM must run on a core the kernel cannot kick, a guest needs AVIC or SEV before those kernel-owned structures are designed, or a guest must span kernel instances.
